Pregnancy

Pregnancy weeks, months and trimesters: making sense of the dates

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy dates can sound contradictory: fifteen weeks pregnant can also mean being in the sixteenth week. A consistent count of completed weeks and days makes the calendar much easier to understand.

Forty weeks is the dating convention

A pregnancy due date is commonly estimated as forty weeks, or 280 days, from the first day of the last menstrual period. This is called gestational dating. The count begins before conception in a typical cycle, so “four weeks pregnant” does not mean fertilisation happened four weeks ago.

The expected due date, often abbreviated EDD, is an estimate rather than an appointment the baby must keep. Birth can occur before or after it. Do not interpret a general percentage about births at forty weeks as a prediction of your own labour date.

The care team uses this shared dating system to plan screening, assess growth and discuss birth timing. Consistency matters more than finding a month label that sounds exact. Once the best clinical estimate is agreed, keep that date in your pregnancy record and any app you use.

Why the count starts with the last period

The first day of the last menstrual period, or LMP, provides a starting point that many people can identify. In a typical twenty-eight-day cycle, ovulation and fertilisation occur around two weeks later. This explains why the first two gestational weeks are included even though conception has usually not yet happened.

The LMP is not the actual day of conception. Ovulation can occur earlier or later, especially with irregular cycles. A bleed may also be mistaken for a period, and not everyone remembers the date. These are reasons to assess dating carefully rather than assume the calendar method must be right.

The date of intercourse does not necessarily identify fertilisation either: sperm can remain available for several days, whereas the released egg has a shorter fertilisable interval. Around the time a period is missed in a regular cycle, the gestational count is often about four weeks. That is an approximation, not a rule for every cycle.

How to calculate an initial due date

For a cycle-based estimate, take the first day of the last period and add 280 days. A traditional shortcut, often called Naegele’s rule, subtracts three calendar months, adds seven days and then adds a year. It assumes a roughly twenty-eight-day cycle and is only an initial estimate.

For example, an LMP beginning on 2 June 2026 gives an estimated due date of 9 March 2027 when 280 days are added. Written month names avoid confusing day/month and month/day formats. Calendar shortcuts can behave differently around month ends, so a day-based calculation is clearer than improvised arithmetic.

Tell the clinician about a longer, shorter or irregular cycle and uncertainty over the period date. If you conceived with assisted reproduction, use the fertility clinic’s dating based on the treatment and embryo information. Do not replace that with a remembered bleed or treat embryo-transfer day as gestational day zero.

Completed weeks and the week you are in

Clinical records usually state completed weeks and additional days. Fifteen weeks and three days may be written as 15+3 or 15w3d. It means fifteen full weeks have passed and you are three days into the next one. It does not mean fifteen-point-three weeks as a decimal.

This is why “fifteen weeks pregnant” and “in the sixteenth week” can describe the same stage. The first counts completed weeks; the second names the week currently unfolding. At 16+0, sixteen full weeks have been completed.

The distinction is similar to a birthday: after a first birthday, a child is one year old and living through their second year. Pregnancy apps sometimes use different labels, so compare the actual weeks-and-days count and due date before assuming two records disagree. For appointments and medical questions, use the completed count.

Where the three trimesters begin and end

A commonly used clinical framework defines the first trimester from the start of the gestational count through 13 weeks and 6 days. The second runs from 14 weeks and 0 days through 27 weeks and 6 days. The third begins at 28 weeks and 0 days and continues until birth.

The divisions are not three perfectly equal thirteen-week blocks. Forty does not divide evenly into three whole weeks, and pregnancy does not necessarily end precisely at 40+0. A third trimester does not disappear if pregnancy continues after the estimated date.

Some patient materials use slightly different boundary labels. This is usually a difference in presentation, not a change in the baby’s age. Use your service’s exact gestational window when booking a test rather than relying on a broad phrase such as “the end of the first trimester.”

Why forty weeks is about nine calendar months

Four weeks equal twenty-eight days, but most calendar months have thirty or thirty-one days. Dividing forty by four therefore produces ten blocks of four weeks, not ten ordinary calendar months. A calendar month averages a little more than four weeks.

This is why pregnancy can be described conversationally as about nine months while the clinical count is forty weeks from the LMP. Neither phrase tells you the exact conception date. Counting from likely fertilisation gives a shorter interval than counting from the last period.

For family conversations, a rough month label is usually enough. For medication timing, scan windows, growth assessments or birth planning, it is not. Keep the weeks-and-days notation available so that a casual month description does not become an unintended medical instruction.

An approximate month guide, with clear limits

One familiar reading guide groups numbered pregnancy weeks as follows: month one, weeks 1–4; month two, weeks 5–8; month three, weeks 9–13. These are approximate week labels for following a guide, not exact calendar-month anniversaries.

The same guide continues with month four, weeks 14–17; month five, weeks 18–22; month six, weeks 23–27. It then uses month seven, weeks 28–31; month eight, weeks 32–35; and month nine, weeks 36–40.

Other charts divide the weeks differently, and a pregnancy may continue beyond the last block. An app’s “week sixteen” may mean the sixteenth week in progress rather than sixteen completed weeks. This chart must not be used to schedule tests; the confirmed EDD and completed weeks plus days remain the more precise reference.

Preterm, early term and full term have specific meanings

A preterm birth occurs before 37 weeks and 0 days. For births from 37 weeks onward, ACOG distinguishes early term at 37+0 through 38+6, full term at 39+0 through 40+6, late term at 41+0 through 41+6, and postterm from 42+0 onward.

Early term is not the same as preterm, and reaching 37 weeks does not mean every aspect of development is identical to 39 weeks. These categories help describe timing and risks; they do not predict exactly how an individual baby will do.

The due date is 40+0, within the full-term interval. Passing that date does not by itself mean something has gone wrong, but it does call for the planned discussion of monitoring and birth options. Follow your maternity team’s advice rather than waiting for a chart to reach its final week.

Twins do not have a universal thirty-eight-week minimum

Twin pregnancies are dated in weeks and days using the same gestational convention, but their birth plan often differs from a singleton pregnancy. Whether the babies share a placenta or an amniotic sac, their growth and any complications influence the recommended timing.

For example, NICE recommends planned birth at thirty-seven weeks for uncomplicated twins with separate placentas and sacs, and at thirty-six weeks for uncomplicated twins sharing a placenta but with separate sacs. Twins sharing a sac and complicated pregnancies need different specialist plans.

These examples are guidance within a particular care system, not dates to choose without your own team. “Twins are full term only after at least thirty-eight weeks” is not a safe general rule. An earlier recommended birth can be an intentional balance of risks rather than evidence that the pregnancy was dated incorrectly.

Use the best clinical date and ask about apparent changes

An early ultrasound can establish or confirm gestational age, especially when the LMP is uncertain or does not fit the measurements. First-trimester ultrasound is generally the most accurate ultrasound stage for dating. The team combines the available information rather than assuming every new estimate should replace the last.

Later scans often describe the size of a body part in relation to an average gestational age. A measurement labelled “two weeks ahead” does not necessarily mean conception happened two weeks earlier. Growth assessment and redating are different questions, and unnecessary date changes can obscure a growth concern.

Ask which EDD is the agreed one, how it was established and whether a reported difference changes your care plan. Update an app only when the clinical date is actually changed. If symptoms worry you, contact the maternity service regardless of what a week, month or trimester label says.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Gestational dating commonly starts at the last period, not the day of conception.

Month charts are approximate; clinical care uses weeks and days.

Early ultrasound or fertility-treatment information may refine the initial estimate.

How BeMama can help

Keep one agreed due date in your pregnancy record and app, together with how it was established. Use a format such as 15 weeks and 3 days when discussing appointments.

When to seek help

Follow the maternity team’s timing for screening, monitoring and birth. Do not delay advice about concerning symptoms because a calendar label suggests they are too early or too late.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Forty weeks equal 280 days, not ten calendar months.
  • 15+3 means fifteen completed weeks and three days.
  • Full term runs from 39+0 through 40+6.
  • Twins need an individual birth plan, not a universal 38-week minimum.
  • Later size measurements do not automatically change the due date.

Frequently asked questions

Is the first day of my last period the day I conceived?

No. It is the conventional starting point for gestational dating, usually before conception.

How can I be four weeks pregnant when conception was more recent?

The usual count includes about two weeks before fertilisation in a typical cycle.

What does 15+3 mean?

Fifteen completed weeks and three additional days; you are in the sixteenth week.

Does forty weeks mean ten months?

It means ten four-week blocks, but about nine calendar months because most months are longer than twenty-eight days.

When does the second trimester start?

In the framework used here it begins at 14 weeks and 0 days; use exact service-specific windows for tests.

Can a month chart tell me when to book a scan?

No. Month charts are approximate. Use the confirmed weeks-and-days count and your service’s instructions.

Is 37 weeks full term?

It is early term. Full term is 39 weeks and 0 days through 40 weeks and 6 days.

Must twins stay in the womb until at least 38 weeks?

No. Recommended timing depends on placenta and sac arrangements, complications and the individual specialist plan.

Should I calculate from embryo-transfer day as day zero?

No. Use the fertility clinic’s gestational dating, which accounts for embryo age and treatment details.

Does measuring ahead on a later scan change my due date?

Not automatically. Ask whether the finding describes growth or a genuine change to the agreed clinical dating.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
